payload.claim: `restore_mutant` locates where to reinsert the displaced bytes by requiring `content.count(mutant.replace.encode()) == 1`, but `Mutant.replace` defaults to `""` (saffron/intake.py:62) and is schema-legal as empty — a deletion mutant (find text removed, nothing put in its place). Python's `bytes.count(b"")` returns `len(content) + 1`, not 1, for any non-empty file, so for every deletion mutant `restore_mutant` will raise `MutationError` deterministically rather than restoring the file, even though `apply_mutant` succeeds and returns a valid `displaced` value for exactly this case. This breaks the acceptance criterion that applying and restoring must leave the file byte-identical, for a mutant shape (delete a guard/check) that is arguably the most natural kind of mutant to write, and it is untested: every case in tests/test_mutation.py uses a non-empty `replace="x"`.
